title: Separating the body and chassis of a Citroën 2CV4: why this dismantling step decides the whole project
author: Caramagnols
excerpt: On this 2CV4, the real restoration started when the body came off the chassis. As long as both remain assembled, it is hard to see what still holds and what will need deeper work.
content:
In the workshop, the restoration of this 2CV4 did not begin with cleaning or with an optimistic attempt to start the engine. The decisive moment came when the body was separated from the chassis. On a simple car like a 2CV, that can look obvious. In reality, it turns a buying impression into a precise diagnosis, because it forces you to examine separately what still carries weight and what no longer does.

Why this step cannot be skipped

As long as the car stays assembled, part of the damage remains hidden. Floor panels mask older repairs, the shell hides weak points underneath and the chassis can look stronger than it really is while still under the car. On our 2CV4 in Rioz, separation was the moment when estimation had to give way to proof.

This dismantling is therefore not a workshop luxury. It is a structural check. It tells you whether the next phase will involve a few local repairs or a much broader rebuild of the underside. Without it, both the budget and the work order stay vague.

What the chassis revealed

Once isolated, the chassis of this 2CV4 proved recoverable. That matters because it avoids rebuilding the entire rolling base from zero. The reading was no longer a chassis assumed to be sound, but a part that had been seen, checked and judged solid enough to justify serious work.

That kind of finding changes the whole project immediately. If the chassis still holds, the effort can be focused on the truly dead areas of the body and underside. If it is lost, the restoration changes scale and cost from the first day.

What the body was still hiding

By contrast, the shell proved more damaged than the first walk-around had suggested. The floors were dead, the sills badly affected and some earlier repairs had mainly hidden corrosion instead of solving it. Without separation, those defects would have remained partly invisible and therefore easier to underestimate.

That is exactly why dismantling decides the project. It is not done to make things look neat; it is done to show where illusion ends and real work starts. On a 2CV, a few tired panels are normal. An underside that was previously repaired badly calls for a much heavier level of intervention.

Deciding the next steps from facts

Once body and chassis are apart, the restoration stops being vague. Decisions are taken from facts: chassis checked, floors to replace, sills to rebuild, lower half-bulkhead perforated, tank surroundings to treat. That concrete list then sets the correct order for metal work, protection and later mechanical recommissioning.

The full project overview remains on the parent page Citroën 2CV4 Restoration by Garage SAVA - Rioz. The draft devoted to the order of structural metal work follows directly from this first step.
